text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF
BRITISH
COLUMBIA

Citation:

Carson v. Knucwentwecw Society,

2006 BCSC 1779

Date: 20061201

Docket:
S-063522

Registry: Vancouver

In the Matter of the
Human Rights Code
,

R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210 (as amended)

And in the Matter of a Decision made by the British Columbia

Human Rights Tribunal on April 3, 2006

And in the Matter of the
Judicial Review Procedure Act
,

R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 241 (as amended)

Between:

Kelly Carson, Stephen Dickens, Jeff
Dimarco

Joe Dimarco, Anthony Bowser and Nancy Harding

Petitioners

And

Gerald Koehler on behalf of the
Knucwentwecw Society, The Members of the

Knucwentwecw Society, The Members of the Bands whom the Society represents as
individuals upon whose behalf the complaint is being brought

and The Youth who will potentially reside in the facility established by the

Society at 3023 De Sous Mountain Road in Williams Lake, B.C.

Respondents

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Ehrcke

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Petitioners

Thomas
F. Beasley

Counsel for the Respondents

Catherine
J. Boies Parker

Counsel for the British Columbia Human
Rights Tribunal

Katherine
A. Hardie

Appearing on her own behalf

Twilite
Craige

Date and Place of Trial/Hearing:

October
22 - 23, 2006

Vancouver,
B.C.

Introduction

[
1
]

This petition concerns a complaint that was made
to the British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal (the “Tribunal”) against the
present six petitioners and Twilite Craige (whom I shall refer to collectively
as the “Seven Respondents”).  Prior to the hearing, the Seven Respondents
brought a preliminary application to summarily dismiss the complaint against
them.  The Tribunal dismissed that application in reasons indexed as
Koehler
v. Carson and Others (No. 2)
,
2006 BCHRT 178
.  The petitioners now
apply, pursuant to the
Judicial Review Procedure Act
, R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 241, for judicial review of that decision.  Although not named as
one of the petitioners, Twilite Craige appeared and made submissions before me
in support of the petition.

The Facts and the Relevant Statutory
Provisions

[
2
]

The Knucwentwecw Society (the “Society”) is a
First Nations Child and Family Services Agency providing services to children,
youth and families of four Caribou Tribal Council Member Bands.  It purchased
two private lots on De Sous Mountain Road, approximately 25 kilometres west of
Williams Lake for the purpose of developing a care home for six adolescent
boys.  Some residents of the area object to the location of the proposed care
home.  Many of them posted signs, wrote letters to the newspaper, and made
statements at meetings expressing their concerns.  It was the nature of these
signs, letters, and statements that led to a complaint being filed with the
Tribunal.

[
3
]

The complaint was initially filed by Doreen
Johnson as a representative complainant on behalf of the Society, members of
the Society, and youth who will reside at the facility.  Representative
complaints are specifically provided for in
s. 21(4)
of the
Code
.
The complaint alleged that the Seven Respondents, Kelly Carson, Stephen
Dickens, Jeff Dimarco, Joe Dimarco, Twilite Craige, Anthony Bowser and Nancy
Harding, made publications that discriminated against them on the basis of
race, colour, ancestry, family status, physical disability and mental
disability, contrary to
s. 7
of the
Human Rights Code
, R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 210 (the “
Code
”) which provides:

7  (1)  A person
must not publish, issue or display, or cause to be published, issued or
displayed, any statement, publication, notice, sign, symbol, emblem or other
representation that

(a) indicates discrimination or an
intention to discriminate against a person or a group or class of persons, or

(b) is likely to expose a person or a
group or class of persons to hatred or contempt

because of the
race, colour, ancestry, place of origin, religion, marital status, family
status, physical or mental disability, sex, sexual orientation or age of that
person or that group or class of persons.

(2)  Subsection
(1) does not apply to a private communication or to a communication intended to
be private.

[
4
]

More specifically, the complaint alleges that
each of the Seven Respondents is responsible for publications implying that the
youth, the Society, and its members are inferior, dangerous, and pose a threat
to the community because of their race, colour, ancestry, family status and
mental and physical disability.  The complainants also say that the
publications are likely to expose them to hatred and contempt.

[
5
]

The Seven Respondents denied that they had
discriminated, and they filed an application to dismiss the complaint on a
preliminary basis pursuant to
ss. 27(1)
(a), (b), and (c) of the
Code
,
which provides:

27  (1)  A member
or panel may, at any time after a complaint is filed and with or without a
hearing, dismiss all or part of the complaint if that member or panel
determines that any of the following apply:

(a) the complaint or that part of the
complaint is not within the jurisdiction of the tribunal;

(b) the acts or omissions alleged in the
complaint or that part of the complaint do not contravene this
Code
;

(c) there is no reasonable prospect that
the complaint will succeed;

[
6
]

Before that application was decided, the
complainants filed an application to substitute a different person as the
representative complainant and to amend their complaint.  On January 30, 2006,
the Tribunal rendered a decision (
Koehler v. Carson and Others
,

2006 BCHRT 50
) allowing the substitution and amendment, so that Gerald Koehler
is now the representative complainant on behalf of the Society, members of the
Society, members of the Bands whom the Society represents, and the youth who
will reside at the facility.  None of the Seven Respondents have made any
application to review that decision.

[
7
]

On April 3, 2006, the Tribunal dismissed the
application of the Seven Respondents for summary dismissal.  The Tribunal
rejected their argument under
s. 27(1)
(a) that the complaint was not
within the Tribunal’s jurisdiction, their argument under
s. 27(1)
(b) that the
acts complained of do not contravene the
Code
, and their argument
under
s. 27(1)
(c) that the complaint has no reasonable prospect of success.  The
petitioners now seek to have that decision set aside.  They say that the
Tribunal erred in its application of each of
ss. 27(1)
(a), (b), and (c) of the
Code
.

The Standard of Review

[
8
]

The standard of judicial review for decisions of
the Tribunal is governed by
s. 59
of the
Administrative Tribunals
Act
, S.B.C. 2004, c. 45, which provides:

59  (1)  In a
judicial review proceeding, the standard of review to be applied to a decision
of the tribunal is correctness for all questions except those respecting the
exercise of discretion, findings of fact and the application of the common law
rules of natural justice and procedural fairness.

(2)  A court must
not set aside a finding of fact by the tribunal unless there is no evidence to
support it or if, in light of all the evidence, the finding is otherwise
unreasonable.

(3)  A court must
not set aside a discretionary decision of the tribunal unless it is patently
unreasonable.

(4)  For the purposes
of subsection (3), a discretionary decision is patently unreasonable if the
discretion

(a) is exercised arbitrarily or in bad
faith,

(b) is exercised for an improper purpose,

(c) is based entirely or predominantly on
irrelevant factors, or

(d) fails to take statutory requirements
into account.

(5)  Questions
about the application of common law rules of natural justice and procedural
fairness must be decided having regard to whether, in all of the circumstances,
the tribunal acted fairly.

[
9
]

The parties are agreed that the standard of
review for the Tribunal’s decisions concerning jurisdiction under
s. 27(1)
(a)
of the
Code
is correctness.  They also agree that the standard of
review for discretionary decisions under
s. 27(1)
(c) is patent unreasonableness.
In so far as the application of
s. 27(1)
(b) involves an interpretation of the
meaning of
s. 7(1)
of the
Code
, the petitioners and the complainants
agree that the standard is correctness.

The Petitioners’ First Ground for
Judicial Review - Standing

[
10
]

The petitioners’ first argument is that the
complainants lack standing to bring the complaint.  They argue that the
Code

protects personal rights, and the Society therefore cannot be a complainant.

[
11
]

In this case, the complaint is not brought by
the Society directly, but rather, by Gerald Koehler on behalf of the Society
and others.  As mentioned above,
s. 21(4)
of the
Code

specifically provides for such representative complaints.

[
12
]

The Tribunal held that it could not dismiss the
complaint on the basis of the standing argument, since Mr. Koehler clearly had
standing, and that was all that was required.  The Tribunal held at paras. 15 -
16:

15.       I am not
persuaded by the Respondents' arguments in this regard.  The complainant in
this case is Mr. Koehler.  He brings the complaint on behalf of the
Knucwentwecw.

16.       First, I
find that the complaint is brought by a person, Mr. Koehler, on behalf of the
persons defined as the members of the group he represents.  The Knucwentwecw
complaint alleges discrimination on behalf of a group of persons.  I do not
need to determine the issue of whether the youth who will potentially reside in
the facility are properly named, as it is clear that Mr. Koehler, himself if
need be, has standing to bring this complaint and the Tribunal has jurisdiction
to hear it.

[
13
]

The decision to permit Gerald Koehler to be
named as a representative complainant and to add members to the representative
group or class was made in the Tribunal’s previous decision of January 30, 2006.
That decision constitutes a finding that Gerald Koehler is a proper
complainant.  Any objection to his standing should have been brought by an
application to review that decision.  No such application having been made, the
objection cannot succeed.

The Petitioners’ Second Ground -
Jurisdiction

[
14
]

The petitioners’ next argument is that the complaint
falls within exclusive federal jurisdiction, and therefore the Tribunal erred
in failing to dismiss the complaint under
s. 27(1)
(a) of the
Code
.
The petitioners argue that under
s. 91(24)
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
,
the federal government has jurisdiction over “Indians, and lands reserved for
Indians”, and since the present complaint relates to a care home for First
Nations’ adolescents, the British Columbia Provincial Human Rights Tribunal
lacks jurisdiction to hear it.

[
15
]

In this case, the Tribunal is not being asked to
inquire into the activities of any First Nations people; it is not their
conduct that is the subject of the inquiry.  Rather, the subject matter of the
complaint is the activities of the Seven Respondents, who are not Native.  The
question that the Tribunal will have to consider on the hearing of the
complaint, is whether the Seven Respondents breached
s. 7
of the
Code
.
That issue is not one that concerns “Indians, and lands reserved for Indians”.
The Tribunal was correct in rejecting the argument under
s. 27(1)
(a) of the
Code

that it lacked jurisdiction.

[
16
]

The complaint in this case is about publications
by the Seven Respondents.  Their argument that the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction
amounts to a claim that since the content of their publications relates to
Indians, the Province must lack jurisdiction to regulate those publications.  A
similar argument was rejected in an earlier decision of the Tribunal,
Canadian
Jewish Congress v. North Shore Free Press Ltd. (c.o.b. North Shore News)
,
[1997] B.C.H.R.T.D. No. 23 at para. 60:

60        The
proposition that jurisdiction to regulate speech is divided in the manner
suggested has no support whatsoever in the jurisprudence.  Speech is a matter
of divided jurisdiction but the division concerns the nature and purpose of the
regulation (that is, its "aspect"), not the topic of the particular
speech in issue:
Attorney-General (Canada) and Dupond v. Montreal
,

1978 CanLII 201 (SCC)
, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 770 at 796-7.  (See also
Nova Scotia Board of Censors v.
McNeil
,
1978 CanLII 6 (SCC)
, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 662 at 688 where the Court held that provincial
legislative authority to restrict the public viewing of films was not
diminished in the case of films imported from another country.)
Regulation
of speech about "Indians", who are assigned to exclusive federal
jurisdiction by
s. 91(24)
, for example, is clearly not beyond the competence of
the province. To suggest otherwise would mean that an individual who was
defamed by speech that focused on his or her aboriginal status could not seek a
civil remedy under the
Libel and Slander Act
.  Similarly, provincial
regulation of advertising could not encompass advertising concerning the postal
service (assigned to federal jurisdiction by s. 91(5)).  Such an approach
to jurisdiction over speech is inconsistent with the pith and substance
doctrine which underlies division of powers analysis and enables a government
to enact laws with a substantial impact on matters outside its jurisdiction as
long as it the law itself is generally found to be "in relation to"
one of the heads of power assigned to that level of government.  (See generally

Hogg
,
supra
, at 378-9 and the numerous authorities cited in the
accompanying notes.)

[Emphasis Added]

[
17
]

The fact that the complaint in the present case
was brought by Native people, and that it is their desire to build a care home
that prompted the allegedly discriminatory publications, does not
constitutionally immunize the conduct of the of the non-Native Seven
Respondents from scrutiny by the British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal.

[
18
]

At para. 50 of their written argument, the
petitioners submit:

The Tribunal’s
decision leads to an absurd conclusion, being that the Canadian Human Rights
Commission (“CHRC”) would have jurisdiction with respect to services offered by
the Treatment Home and employment at the Treatment Home, but the Tribunal would
have jurisdiction with respect to discriminatory publications concerning the
Treatment Home.

[
19
]

Suffice it to say that if the alleged conclusion
referred to by the petitioners indeed follows from the Tribunal’s decision, I
do not find it to be absurd.  If that conclusion is considered by some to be
unpalatable, then that is a result of Canada’s constitutional framework; it is
not a result of any defect in the Tribunal’s reasoning.

[
20
]

The standard of review on the issue of
jurisdiction is correctness.  I am satisfied that the Tribunal was correct in
concluding that it had jurisdiction over this complaint.

The Petitioners’ Third Ground –
Field of Activity

[
21
]

The Seven Respondents argued before the Tribunal
that the complaint under
s. 7(1)
(a) of the
Code
should be
dismissed because it alleges discrimination, without alleging that the
discrimination is in respect of a field of activity otherwise covered by the
Code
.
The Tribunal considered this as an argument to dismiss under
s. 27(1)
(b), since
it raises the question of whether reference to a field of activity is an
essential element which must be established under
s. 7(1)
(a).  I agree that
that is the proper approach.

[
22
]

The petitioners argue that s. 7(1)(a) does not
prohibit all forms of discriminatory publication, but only such as are discriminatory
in a respect of a field of activity otherwise protected by the
Code
.
As they put it in their written argument at para. 55:

Nor is it
discriminatory for a person to write a Letter to the Editor stating that “I do
not like X coloured people.”  That is their civil right.  It becomes
discrimination when that civil right moves beyond their opinion to
discrimination with respect to the matter covered under the
Code
, being
a field of activity under the
Code
, such as employment, public services,
membership in a trade union, etc.

[
23
]

The petitioners rely on a previous decision of
the Tribunal,
Stacey v. Campbell
,
2002 BCHRT 35
, which
interpreted
s. 7(1)
(a) as not prohibiting all forms of discrimination, but only
publications “that indicates discrimination or an intention to discriminate
with respect to the fields of activity that are covered by the other sections
of the
Code
”:  see
Stacey
at paras.
27 - 34
.

[
24
]

The petitioners also rely on
Khanna v.
Common Ground Publishing
,
2005 BCHRT 398
, in which the Tribunal followed

Stacey
and dismissed a complaint on the ground that the alleged
discriminatory publication did not have “either a discriminatory effect, or an
intended a discriminatory effect, with respect to the areas protected by the

Code
”: see
Khanna
at para.
34
.

[
25
]

In the present case, the Tribunal concluded that
it is not essential under
s. 7(1)
(a) for a complaint to allege that the
publication was discriminatory with respect to an area otherwise protected by
the
Code
.  In coming to that conclusion, the Tribunal
acknowledged that it was departing from the interpretation of that section
adopted in
Stacey
.

[
26
]

The petitioners submit that the Tribunal in the
present case erred in failing to follow previous Tribunal decisions.  That in
itself, however, is not an error.  Tribunal members are not bound by previous
decisions of the Tribunal, although it is a rare case when a Tribunal member
will not defer to an interpretation previously adopted by a Tribunal.  This is
one of those rare cases.

[
27
]

The petitioners and the complainants agree that
the standard of review on this issue is correctness.  The question before me is
whether the Tribunal in this case was correct in deciding that it is not
essential under
s. 7(1)
(a) for a complaint to allege that a publication was
discriminatory with respect to an area otherwise protected by the
Code
,
notwithstanding that this decision departed from previous Tribunal decisions
such as
Stacey
.

[
28
]

The Tribunal in the present case engaged in a
careful analysis of the reasoning in
Stacey
.  It noted that the
decision in
Stacey
referred to
Ukrainian Canadian
Professional and Business Association v. Konyk
(1982),
1982 CanLII 4863 (BC HRT)
, 3 C.H.R.R.
D/1157 (B.C. Bd. of Inq.), aff'd (1983),
1983 CanLII 4701 (BC SC)
, 4 C.H.R.R. D/1653 (B.C.S.C.), which
turned on the interpretation of s. 2 of the former
Human Rights Code
,
R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 186.  That section, which has since been repealed, was
worded differently from the present
s. 7(1)
(a).  Section 2(1) of the former
Code

provided:

2(1)  No person
shall publish or display before the public, or cause to be published or
displayed before the public, a notice, sign, symbol, emblem or other
representation
indicating discrimination or an intention to discriminate
against a person or class of persons in any manner prohibited by this Act
.

[Emphasis Added]

[
29
]

The current s. 7(1)(a) contains no limiting
words comparable to the underlined words of the former
Code

section.

[
30
]

The Tribunal in the present case noted that the
decision in
Stacey
referred to a number of decisions from other
jurisdictions that applied a similar interpretation notwithstanding the absence
of the limiting words:
Singer v. Iwasyk
, (November 5, 1976),
(unreported),
Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission, Engineering Students'
Society, University of Saskatchewan v. Saskatchewan (Human Rights Board of
Inquiry)
,
1989 CanLII 286 (SK CA)
, [1989] S.J. No. 35, (1989), 10 C.H.R.R. D/5636 (Sask. C.A.),
Black
United Front v. Bramhill
(1980),
1980 CanLII 3926 (NS HRC)
, 2 C.H.R.R. D/249 (N.S. Bd. of Inq.)
and
Kane v. Alberta Report
(2002), C.H.R.R. Doc. 02-079 (Alta.
H.R.P.).  The Tribunal then went on to analyze those cases and concluded that
they do not necessarily support the interpretation placed upon them in
Stacey
.

[
31
]

Moreover, the Tribunal noted that
Stacey

did not consider an Alberta case which came to the conclusion that a provision of
their Act comparable to s. 7(1)(a) of our
Code
did not restrict
discrimination in publication to a field of activity otherwise covered:
Kane
v. Church of Jesus Christ Christian-Aryan Nations (No. 3)
(1993)
C.H.R.R. D/268 at para. 308.

[
32
]

Accordingly, the Tribunal in the present case
determined that a plain language interpretation should be placed on s.
7(1)(a).  As that section has no limiting words, and as the
Code

ought to be construed purposively, the Tribunal concluded that the limitation
adopted in
Stacey
should not be read in.  The Tribunal concluded
at para. 50:

50        Therefore,
to determine whether a complaint is justified under
s. 7(1)
(a) of the
Code
,
the Tribunal is required to determine whether a person has published, issued or
displayed, any statement, publication, notice, sign, symbol, emblem or other
representation that indicates discrimination or an intention to discriminate
against a person or a group or class of persons because of one or more of the
grounds protected under this provision.  Section 7(2) indicates that subsection
(1) does not apply to a private communication or to a communication intended to
be private.

[
33
]

In my respectful opinion, the Tribunal correctly
interpreted
s. 7(1)
(a) and correctly determined that the complaint in this case
should not be dismissed under
s. 27(1)
(b).

The Petitioners’ Fourth Ground –
No Reasonable Prospect of Success

[
34
]

The Seven Respondents also submitted to the Tribunal
that the complaint should be dismissed under either
s. 27(1)
(b) or (c) on the
basis that there was no reasonable prospect that it would succeed.  The
petitioners and Ms. Craige submit that the Tribunal erred in failing to
properly analyze the record to determine this issue.  They submit that the
Tribunal was required to, but did not, engage in an individual analysis of the record
as it relates to each of the Seven Respondents.

[
35
]

The Tribunal’s decision on this issue is found
at paras. 54-59:

54        Section
27(1)(b) provides for the dismissal of complaints which fail to allege acts or
omissions which could contravene the
Code
.  An act or omission which may
be a contravention of the
Code
requires a nexus or connection between
the allegedly unfair treatment and a prohibited ground of discrimination under
the
Code
:
Ingram v. Workers' Compensation Board and others
,
2003
BCHRT 57
, at para.
20
.

55        An
application to dismiss pursuant to
s. 27(1)
(c) is not a determination of
whether a complainant has established a
prima facie
case of
discrimination, nor to determine the
bona fides
of the response:
Wickham
and Wickham v. Mesa Contempoary Folk Art and others
,
2004 BCHRT 134
at
para.
11
.
Section 27(1)
(c) of the
Code
requires the respondent to
establish that there is no reasonable prospect that the complaint will succeed.
The Tribunal makes this assessment on the basis of all of the material before
it.

56        The
Respondents' application to dismiss the complaint pursuant to
s. 27(1)
(b) of
the
Code
is based on submissions relevant to each named respondent.  In
each case, the submissions either deny the veracity of facts alleged in Mr.
Koehler's complaint, assert a non-discriminatory intent, or state that the
alleged conduct was a collaborative, not an individual, effort.

57        Mr.
Koehler alleges that the publications made by the Respondents made pejorative
comments about the Knucwentwecw based on protected grounds and therefore
constitute discrimination contrary to
s. 7(1)
(a) of the
Code
.  He
further alleges that the Respondents discriminated contrary to s. 7(1)(b) of
the
Code
when they engaged in mounting a campaign of discriminatory
publications that perpetuated stereotypical assumptions about First Nations
persons and thereby likely exposed the Knucwentwecw to hatred or contempt.  His
allegations of discrimination include a nexus between the alleged conduct and
the alleged discrimination and extend to matters covered by the
Code
.  The
Respondents' submissions provide a different version of the facts; they do not
establish that Mr. Koehler's allegations of discrimination are not a
contravention of the
Code
.  The Respondents' application to dismiss
pursuant to
s. 27(1)
(b) of the
Code
is denied.

58        The
essence of the Respondents' application to dismiss pursuant to
s. 27(1)
(c) is that,
on the whole of the material currently before the Tribunal, it is evident that
there is no reasonable prospect the complaint will succeed.  In support, they
submit that the Respondents' alleged conduct, if it occurred, was based on
safety concerns; that there was no discriminatory intent, and that the
threshold of proof respecting "hate publications" is a high standard
that Mr. Koehler has failed to meet, and has no reasonable prospect of meeting.
The Respondents filed submissions and a copy of the Society's Constitution and
incorporation documents in support of their application to dismiss, but no
affidavit evidence.

59        I am not
persuaded by the Respondents' submissions that there is no reasonable prospect
Mr. Koehler's complaint will succeed. Intent is not necessary to a finding of a
breach of the
Code
.  A
s. 27(1)
(c) application does not require Mr.
Koehler to establish a
prima facie
case of discrimination:
Bell v.
Dr. Sherk and others
,
2003 BCHRT 63
at para.
29
.  The parties' submissions
demonstrate different views respecting the facts.  A determination requires
contextual findings of fact.  A hearing provides the opportunity to adduce
individual and expert evidence, and documentary evidence, and the opportunity
to test that evidence through cross-examination.  A hearing is required to
determine the allegations made in Mr. Koehler's complaint.  The Respondents'
application to dismiss this complaint pursuant to
s. 27(1)
(c) is denied.

[
36
]

I agree with the Tribunal that it cannot be
concluded on the current record that the complaints against any of the Seven
Respondents either fail to amount to a contravention of the
Code

or that there is no reasonable prospect that they will succeed.  To determine
the validity of the complaints, evidence will be required to give context to
the publications.  The discriminatory nature of a publication is not
necessarily apparent simply by considering the words used, in the absence of
any context.  This point was eloquently expressed in
Abrams v. North
Shore Free Press Ltd. (c.o.b. North Shore News)
, [1999] B.C.H.R.T.D.
No. 5 at para. 59:

In my view,
context is critical in understanding the meaning of a message.  The meaning
conveyed by an expression may vary depending on its context.  An expression
that appears neutral or innocuous out of context may take on a very different
meaning when put in its proper context.  Context for this purpose includes not
only the publication context but also the social and historical contexts.

[
37
]

Finally, it should be noted that a determination
of whether the complaint has any reasonable prospect of success involves the
exercise of discretion.  Pursuant to
s. 59(3)
of the
Administrative
Tribunals Act
, a court must not set aside such a decision unless it is
patently unreasonable.  What is meant by patent unreasonableness in this
context is set out in s. 59(4):

59 (4)  For the
purposes of subsection (3), a discretionary decision is patently unreasonable
if the discretion

(a) is exercised arbitrarily or in bad
faith,

(b) is exercised for an improper purpose,

(c) is based entirely or predominantly on
irrelevant factors, or

(d) fails to take statutory requirements
into account.

[
38
]

There is nothing before me to suggest that the
Tribunal exercised its discretion arbitrarily, in bad faith or for an improper
purpose, or that its decision was based on irrelevant factors or that it failed
to take statutory requirements into account.  In short, its decision not to
dismiss the complaint as having no reasonable prospect of success was not
patently unreasonable.

Conclusion

[
39
]

I have concluded that none of the grounds for
judicial review of the Tribunal’s decision in this case can succeed.
Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

[
40
]

It should be understood that the matter under
review is not a decision that there has been a violation of the
Code
;
rather, it is simply a decision that the complaints should not be dismissed on
a preliminary basis before there has been a hearing.

[
41
]

The Seven Respondents will still have a full
opportunity to present whatever evidence and arguments they consider relevant
when this matter comes to hearing before the Tribunal.
